title: API 653 Training in Los Angeles: Tank Inspector Exam Prep
description: Self-paced API 653 exam prep for Los Angeles and Long Beach tank inspectors: harbour terminals, refinery tank farms, AQMD tank rules, seismic details.
h1: API 653 Training in Los Angeles: Online Exam Prep for Harbour Terminal and Refinery Tank Inspectors
html:
API 653 exam prep for tank inspectors in Los Angeles and Long Beach

The twin ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach and the refineries behind them hold a large share of Southern California's petroleum storage: crude and product tanks at harbour terminals, refinery tank farms in El Segundo, Torrance, Carson and Wilmington, pipeline terminal tankage that feeds lines inland, and smaller chemical and biofuel tanks. API 653 is the certification owners and contractors look for in the inspectors who judge whether those tanks can stay in service.

There is no Atlantis classroom in Los Angeles, and Atlantis does not run a tank inspection seminar in the city. Its API 653 course is self-paced and online, with an instructor answering questions as you work through API 653, API 650, RP 575 and the rest of the Body of Knowledge. API sets the eligibility rules, administers the API 653 examination at Prometric test centres and certifies the candidates who pass; Atlantis is not an API-approved training provider.

Harbour terminals and refinery tank farms

The Port of Los Angeles lists liquid bulk terminals run by Kinder Morgan at Berths 118 and 119, PBF Energy at Berths 238 to 240C, Phillips 66 at Berths 148 to 151, Valero at Berth 164 and Vopak at Berths 187 to 190, among others, and the Port of Long Beach has marine oil terminals of its own. Two examples show the range of tank work behind the docks:

FacilityWhat its operator publishesWhat it means for an API 653 inspector
Kinder Morgan Carson Terminal100 acres, 63 tanks, total storage of 5,705,000 barrels, tanks from 9,000 to 178,000 barrels, one ship dock, and links to Berth 118 and to Watson StationLarge field-erected product tanks at a pipeline origin terminal, where shell, floor and roof work is classic API 653 territory
Vopak Terminal Los Angeles, WilmingtonPetroleum products, chemicals and biofuels; tank sizes from 75 to 23,848 cubic metres; four barge berths and three vessel berthsA wide spread of sizes and products, where the inspector has to decide which tanks API 653 fits and which need another standard

The four large refineries that EIA lists for the area in January 2026 (Marathon's Los Angeles refinery at Carson and Wilmington, Chevron El Segundo, PBF Energy's Torrance refinery and Valero's Wilmington refinery) each keep their own crude, intermediate and product tankage. Phillips 66 stopped refining at its Los Angeles refinery in October 2025, and tanks at a closed or converted site still need a decision: clean, inspect and repurpose them, or take them out of service properly.

Large product tanks, small chemical tanks and the right standard

API 653 is written for steel tanks built to API 650 or its predecessor, API 12C, and owners commonly apply it to other field-erected steel tanks. It does not automatically fit everything in a terminal. EPA's guidance on SPCC integrity testing describes API 653 as the standard typically used for field-erected tanks, STI SP001 as aimed mainly at shop-fabricated and small field-erected tanks and portable containers, and API 12R1 as covering tanks in onshore production service. EPA also says the owner, or a registered Professional Engineer, decides which industry standard applies and what personnel qualifications and test frequencies follow from it.

For a candidate, the lesson is practical. Learn the scope of API 653 well enough to say when a small shop-built tank or a non-steel chemical vessel belongs under a different standard, because an inspector who signs an API 653 report for the wrong tank creates a problem for the owner. The STI SP001 versus API 653 page sets out the dividing lines.

The rules that send an inspector to a Los Angeles tank

  • SPCC and APSA. The federal SPCC rule, 40 CFR 112.8(c)(6), requires each aboveground container to be tested or inspected for integrity on a regular schedule and whenever material repairs are made. California's Aboveground Petroleum Storage Act brings facilities with 1,320 gallons or more of aboveground petroleum storage, or that are subject to 40 CFR 112, under a state programme overseen by the Office of the State Fire Marshal and run locally by Unified Program Agencies, and those facilities must prepare and follow an SPCC plan.
  • Pipeline breakout tanks. Under 49 CFR 195.432, operators inspect the physical integrity of in-service steel breakout tanks to API 653, without its risk-based alternative internal interval. PHMSA oversees interstate pipelines, and the State Fire Marshal oversees intrastate hazardous liquid pipelines in California.
  • Refinery process safety. Where tankage forms part of a covered refinery process, it falls within the mechanical integrity programme the owner runs under Cal/OSHA's refinery process safety standard, title 8 section 5189.1, which calls for inspections that meet or exceed recognized and generally accepted good engineering practice.

None of these rules names a particular certification for the person doing the work, so the owner's programme decides when an API 653 inspector is required. The who can inspect SPCC tanks page explains the federal side.

South Coast AQMD tank rules and API 653 work

The South Coast Air Quality Management District adds a layer that tank inspectors elsewhere rarely meet. Rule 1178 applies to aboveground tanks of 75,000 litres (19,815 gallons) or more storing organic liquids at petroleum facilities that emit more than 20 tons a year of VOC, which takes in the large refineries and terminals. As amended in 2023, it requires domed roofs on external floating roof tanks that store organic liquids with a true vapour pressure of 3 psia or more, and on external floating roof tanks permitted to hold more than 97% crude oil. Rim seal and roof opening checks follow fixed schedules carried out by a South Coast AQMD Certified Person: semiannual gap measurements on open external floating roofs, and on domed and internal floating roof tanks a semiannual visual check with an explosimeter reading plus complete gap measurements each time the tank is emptied and degassed, at least once every ten years. Rule 463, the district's general organic liquid storage rule, applies to tanks of 19,815 gallons or more storing organic liquids and to gasoline tanks down to 251 gallons.

Two consequences matter to an API 653 inspector. First, a dome changes the job: the floating roof and its seals are now inspected inside an enclosed vapour space, and the dome's supports put load into the top of the shell, which deserves attention at every external inspection. Second, the air district's seal inspections and the API 653 inspection look at some of the same components for different reasons, so coordinate them when a tank comes out of service rather than opening it twice. For roof and seal detail, see floating roof inspection under API 653.

Earthquake country: seismic details on in-service tanks

Southern California tanks are designed for earthquake loading, today under API 650 Annex E, and the details show up in every inspection: anchor bolts and anchor chairs, the shell-to-bottom junction, the foundation and the freeboard left for liquid to slosh. In service, inspectors look for corroded or loosened anchorage, buckling or distortion near the base of the shell, cracked or settled foundations, and damage to floating roofs and seals from sloshing after a strong earthquake. Settlement surveys follow API 653 Annex B, which the exam does examine; the tank settlement guide works through it.

The examination itself leaves seismic design out: the Body of Knowledge does not expect shell thickness calculations for wind or earthquake loads. A Los Angeles candidate therefore studies seismic details for the job and the API 653 hydrostatic, corrosion and settlement rules for the exam.

Salt air and the external interval: a worked example

EPA's integrity testing guidance notes that containers near saltwater may need more frequent checks because they corrode faster. API 653's interval rules make the same point arithmetically. These figures are for practice and describe no real tank: a terminal product tank is 100 ft in diameter with a maximum liquid level of 40 ft, specific gravity 0.85, plate of unknown specification and a joint efficiency of 1.0 on record.

  1. Minimum thickness of the first course for the whole course: tmin = 2.6 (H − 1) D G ÷ (S E) = 2.6 × 39 × 100 × 0.85 ÷ 23,600 = 0.365 in., using the 23,600 psi allowable stress for unknown material in the bottom two courses.
  2. The lowest first-course reading was 0.448 in. eight years ago and is 0.420 in. now, so the shell corrosion rate N is 0.028 ÷ 8 = 0.0035 in. per year.
  3. Remaining corrosion allowance RCA = 0.420 − 0.365 = 0.055 in.
  4. Ultrasonic thickness interval = the lesser of RCA ÷ 2N and 15 years: 0.055 ÷ 0.007 = 7.9 years.
  5. External inspection by an authorized inspector = the lesser of 5 years and RCA ÷ 4N: 0.055 ÷ 0.014 = 3.9 years.

The salt-air rate pulls the external interval below the familiar five-year figure, and that is the point an exam question would test. Routine in-service inspections by the owner's own people continue at least monthly. The API inspection interval calculator applies the same rules if you want to try other figures.

Routes into API 653 from harbour and refinery jobs

API 653 Annex D combines education with aboveground storage tank experience gained in the last 10 years while employed by, or under contract with, an authorized inspection agency, including at least a year supervising or performing tank inspection. A bachelor's degree in engineering or technology needs one year; a two-year degree or certificate needs two years in tank design, construction, repair, operation or inspection; a high school diploma three; and no formal education five or more. Details are on the API 653 certification requirements page. People who often take this route in the basin include:

  • NDT technicians who scan tank floors and take shell readings for terminal and refinery contractors;
  • tank construction and repair welders and foremen who add an inspection role;
  • terminal operators and maintenance staff at the harbour who already run the monthly in-service checks;
  • air district Certified Persons whose seal inspection work has given them a feel for floating roofs, although API decides whether that work counts as tank inspection experience.

Studying API 653 around terminal operations

Terminal work follows ship arrivals and pipeline schedules rather than office hours, so self-paced study fits it well. A sensible order: learn API 653 itself first, because most closed-book questions come from it; then the API 650 sections the calculations rely on; then RP 575 for inspection practice, RP 571 for the listed mechanisms, RP 651 and RP 652 for cathodic protection and linings, and finally Section IX and Section V. Work the shell, floor and settlement calculations until you can set them up without notes, since the corrosion-rate and interval formulas may be asked closed-book.

When a figure in a terminal's own inspection report does not match your working, send both to the instructor; seeing where the code and a real report part ways teaches more than another practice question. The API 653 tank inspection guide and the API 653 practice questions help between sessions. Prometric lists test centres in and around Los Angeles, and you book your seat once API has accepted your application.

Sponsoring tank inspectors at a Los Angeles terminal

Terminal operators, refinery tank groups and the contractors that clean, repair and inspect tanks in the basin can enrol several API 653 candidates together, or combine API 653 with API 570 for staff who also cover dock lines and manifolds. Each candidate studies at their own pace with the instructor, and fees are quoted on request. Remember that API judges each application separately, so check every candidate's tank experience before booking anyone into a window.

faq.q: Is a South Coast AQMD Certified Person the same as an API 653 inspector?
faq.a: No. A Certified Person has completed the air district's tank self-inspection programme and an approved fugitive emissions compliance inspection programme, and carries out the seal gap, roof opening and vapour checks that Rules 1178 and 463 require. An API 653 inspector holds API's certification and judges the mechanical integrity of the tank: shell, floor, roof, nozzles, foundation and repairs. Some people hold both, but one does not replace the other.

faq.q: Does the API 653 exam test seismic design for California tanks?
faq.a: No. The Body of Knowledge excludes shell thickness calculations for wind and earthquake loads. It does test settlement under Annex B, the shell and floor rules and the interval calculations. In Los Angeles you still need to understand anchor bolts, anchor chairs and the shell-to-bottom region for real inspections, especially after a strong earthquake, but that knowledge comes from work rather than the exam.

faq.q: Do APSA and SPCC rules require an API 653 inspector in Los Angeles?
faq.a: Not by name. The SPCC rule requires integrity testing to an industry standard on a regular schedule, and California's APSA requires covered facilities to prepare and follow an SPCC plan. EPA leaves the choice of standard, and the qualifications that follow from it, to the owner or a registered Professional Engineer. For large field-erected tanks the standard chosen is usually API 653, which then calls for an API 653 inspector.

faq.q: Are the chemical tanks at harbour terminals API 653 tanks?
faq.a: Some are and some are not. API 653 is written for steel tanks built to API 650 or API 12C, so a large field-erected steel tank in chemical service may well fall under it. Small shop-built tanks are often inspected to STI SP001, and tanks of other materials may need a different standard altogether. The owner's inspection programme, or its engineer, makes that call before an inspector is assigned.

faq.q: Does tank floor scanning experience count toward API 653 eligibility?
faq.a: It can, because API counts experience in the inspection of aboveground storage tanks gained with an authorized inspection agency. Floor scanning, shell thickness surveys and supporting a certified inspector all build that record. API reviews the experience you document on the application, so describe your work accurately, and remember that the total years needed depend on your education.

faq.q: Where do Los Angeles and Long Beach candidates sit the API 653 exam?
faq.a: At a Prometric test centre, in person. Prometric lists test centres in and around Los Angeles; you choose a seat after API accepts your application. The day lasts about 7.5 hours, with a closed-book part, a 45-minute lunch and an open-book part using PDFs on screen. Windows and application deadlines are on the API exam schedule page.

faq.q: Can a terminal operator enrol several tank inspectors at once?
faq.a: Yes. Terminal operators and tank contractors can enrol a group, including candidates working towards different API exams, and each person studies at their own pace with the instructor. Fees are quoted on request. Each candidate applies to API individually, so plan exam windows around tank cleaning and out-of-service schedules so that nobody is booked for the exam in the middle of a tank turnaround.
